links.reason: 1985 gives the count (எண்பத்து நான்கெனு நூறாயிரம்) and the cause (நல்வினைத் திண்பற்றுடையவர்) of reaching the body that Naladiyar 34 calls அரும்பெறல் யாக்கை. The quatrain adds the use (cane juice), so each end supplies what the other lacks.

The keeper in 113 boasts of merit (பயனும் பெற்றேன்) but nothing in the verse shows him weighing fear against pleasure; the king's sword is in 112, outside this link. The pair is a shared topic (another's wife) not incompatible claims.

The merchant's 'நோற்றிலேன் நோற்றிலாள்' repeats the penance-and-lack reasoning, but Kural 270's இலர் means the have-nots, and the claim that it 'need not mean the poor' is stretched. This is shared logic, not a limit on the couplet.
Neither verse says the rescuer in 15 is the dog of 14; 'வான் ஆறு இழிந்து ... ஓர் தேவன்' names no prior identity. The note leans on plot knowledge, and this is mere sequence in a patikam list.

409 foretells Tivittan splitting a lion's mouth; 497 only shows the envoy gazing at two princes by the rules of his lore (நூனெறி). Nothing in 497 answers or tests the sign, and the verse is flagged uncertain.

37 makes the city take women's forms (நங்கையர் படிவங் கொண்ட நகரம்); 46 has swans fearing mates gone at anklet sound. The shared theme is women in the city; 37 holds no image of loss, so 'felt as loss' is not a development.

2598 is a narrator's description of enjoyment (விளைபயன் இனிதிற் றுய்த்து) with no claim that pleasure is good, so it is not an incompatible claim with Tirumular's neem image. The epic's later renunciation is outside the verse.
313 names no king, and 'former sacrificer' Maridattan is not in the Tamil; both verses show a king renouncing with kings, a parallel pattern. The teaches rests on facts outside the two verses.

The comparison of Jain and Buddhist lists is real, but lying (பொய்) is in both lists (242 line 1, Mani 127), so 'overlap on killing, theft and lust and differ on the rest' is wrong. Qualifies does not fit; this is a comparison.

1843 says the umbrellas and bowing kings are the gift of நல்வினைத் தெய்வம்; 1997 names a deed that earns that rank (உண்டி கொடுத்தோர் ... குடைகெழு வேந்தர்). The later verse supplies the cause the earlier left general.
219 announces three dreams and 223 tells one; this is a dream and its telling, mostly sequence. The teaches turns on the king's reading at 225, which is not here, and 223 is flagged uncertain.

2034 names the fruit of giving to ascetics (தவத்தரசர்க் கீந்தபயன்), which adds a reward to Kural 42's duty; that gain is true. The epic side gains little, since 2034 already states its own cause, so the pair is mostly illustration.
239 shows Dattai worshipping the king with flowers and says nothing of her mood, so 'anger not allowed to stand' is read in. The pair is plot sequence, anger then marriage.

Kural 734 names hunger, disease and foes as what a land lacks; Pat 13 closes 'நோயொடு பசி இகந்து ... காத்த நாடே' after lines 10-19 show enemy land ruined by the king's anger. The poem adds who secures the absences and that the same king is the destroying enemy next door.

The verses are not incompatible: 1846 has Padumukan's men laughing at a cattle raid; 1871 has the princess teasing the companions as thieves. That the raid was a ruse and the household knew is not in either Tamil.

Both treat women who sell love, and both use தழீஇ, but 78 is a hunting figure (கண் வலை ... தசை தழீஇ உடலம் விட்டிடும்), not a reworking of the Kural's corpse. Reading the corpse as the client is imported.

1465 shows the merchant examining mouth, palms and feet (தேர்ந்தனன்) and deciding, which follows from marks; 1460 lists head, feet, flanks, eyes. The link is story sequence, and the astrologer's sign is outside both verses.
54 names the ஐவகை ஒழுக்கம் taught by the first teachers; 242 gives the five (கொலை, பொய், களவு, பிறன்மனை, பற்று) and adds three abstentions. A name and its content, and the answer is accurate.

1431 mocks bathing (கயமூழ்கிக் கரடி) but gives no replacement of knowledge, vision and conduct in the verse, and Tirumanthiram 509 does not deny outer bathing, it only points inward. Both clauses of gains lean on content not in the Tamil.

Both strip ornament, but 2635 states no claim that conflicts with Siddhar 19's longing; the difference in aim is not a tension. The 'fixed hall and day' the gains clause cites is not in the Siddhar line.

Both mention Evvi's fall, but Pur 233 gives a dawn report of wounds with no bards' gesture, and Ak 115 lines 8-9 depict the bards laying down the harp in worship. The 'known bardic rite' is read into the pair.
No incompatible claim: 3116 is an auspicious cremation, Naladiyar 24 describes the drum beats and carrying of an ordinary corpse. 'Nothing of the person is lost' is not in 3116.
772 has the kings predicting 'சரங்கண் மூழ்கப் பட்டுலாய்க் கிடக்கலுற்றாய்'; 816 has 'மன்னர் மழையிடை மின்னின் ஒய்தா மறைந்தனர்' and Civakan praised. The later verse reverses the prediction.
Both use the eyes-as-arrows image (பகழி), but 1117 does not accept the glance as a prize; it says Kama's eyes-arrows won and his own austerity earned the touch. 'Accepted as the prize' is overread.

Naladiyar 21 says even kings under umbrellas died and none is left over; 249 says the killing kings 'சிலபகல் அன்றி நின்றார் சிலர்' and then 'பிறவி முந்நீர் அழுந்துவர்'. The verse adds a destination and cause, which the quatrain lacks.

Both have a float (புணை) in a pond, but in 1680 it is the king with his queens and in Ak 266 a husband with other women and the wife's oath-grief (எமக்கே அவலம் அன்று). The fairness-by-partner lesson is not drawn in either.

2985 calls நல்வினை விளையுள் a poison and Tirumanthiram 258 makes தவமறம் a boat over the sea of deeds, a real contrast. Jain thought also takes tapas as the crossing, so it depends on reading அறம் as merit; the verse is flagged.

2885 gives the reason (past and future strangers, hence no kin) and Siddhar 55 states the wish with the lotus leaf image. The pair shows reason beside wish, but the shared theme is detachment from kin, not a development.
3120 shows women seeing stain (மாசு) on their bodies; Naladiyar 46 lists the body's parts. The epic does not give the list, so its women get no 'reasoned list of parts'.
1378 already states the rout follows the crown's fall (மணிமுடி வீழ்தலும் ... புறக்கொடுத்தது), so 1377 adds only the blow. It is plot sequence, and 1377 is flagged uncertain.
The husband's account (she sent him for water) does not contradict her story that a Vidyadhara carried her off; both can be true. That the abduction was a lie is not in either Tamil.

1847 holds 'சிறந்தது தவத்தின் மிக்கதின்மை' from the certainty of death, and Kural 46 asks what is gained by going புறத்தாற்றில் if household life is lived in virtue. A real opposition of renunciation and household virtue.

Both show grieving women, but 2923 has them wither on reading the king's intent and Naladiyar 392 has women hear thunder as a drum in absence. Grief 'felt in advance' is a shared theme; gains name nothing specific.

273 says austerity and rule are heavy burdens; Tirumanthiram 1464 says kings and ascetics have fallen and siddhas come in love. Nothing says those who fell bore the burdens, or that 'weight is not the end'.
Both recall the elephant and Gunamalai, a callback within the epic. 'A joke turned into a debt' is read in; 2957's speaker and sense are uncertain.

Both treat a glance that avoids looking, but Kural 1095 is a lover's clue (ஒருகண் சிறக்கணித்தாள்) and 1295 is a figure of binding (யாத்திட்டாள்). The epic does not show the Kural as its known convention.

The pair joins two uses of நகு- only by a commentator's gloss (Parimelazhagar), which this grading disallows. 784's நகுதல் is merriment in friendship and 860's நகல் is amity opposed to இகல், so the valuations do not conflict.

Naladiyar 101 says the old deed finds its doer as a calf finds its mother; 296 shows 'தொல்லைவினை நின்று சுடுகின்ற நரகத்துள்'. The epic shows what the deed does on arrival, which the quatrain leaves open.

Both set grief beside joy (துயரக் கடல் and இன்பக் கடல்; dirge and wedding drum), but 2356 names no cause, so it does not make 'one man's victory' the cause. A human act in place of an unkind maker is not in the verse.

Valayapathi 57 says the courtesans' service resembles chaste wives' (பத்தினிப் பெண்டிர் படியும் புரைப) for pay; Naladiyar 385 places the difference in the wife's renewed shyness against those who embrace many chests 'பொருள்நசையால்'. A true qualification of the resemblance.

203 has Kattiyankaran vow to bear the yoke 'பழி படா வகையில்' and 241 has him blame a hostile deity and ask how to kill the king. The later verse reverses the vow; the link to 213 is outside this pair.

Both guard the five senses, but 962 uses a fence (ஐம்பொறின் வேலி) in a farm allegory, not the Kural's goad and seed. The answer on வரன் rests on a commentator's gloss, so it is not shown by the Tamil.
Both claim union (ஆவி ஒன்று இரண்டு உடம்பு; உடம்பொடு உயிரிடை), but the 'hollowness' and the other woman's portrait are not in the verse. 'பாவை' here addresses her, not a portrait.
